turns.content: Julian took my bike without asking. Took it to some trail. Left me stranded before my 4:00 shift. I padlocked the garage so he can't pull this again. Maya's stroller is in there. I need to get to work. What do I do.

That’s frustrating—Julian took your transportation without asking, and now you’re stuck trying to make your shift. **Focus on getting to work first; deal with the boundary afterward.**

1. **Text Julian:** “I need my bike to get to my 4:00 shift. Bring it back now and tell me your ETA. If you can’t get it here in time, I need you to arrange or cover a ride.”
2. **Line up a backup now:** a coworker, friend, bus, taxi, or rideshare—whichever is available and affordable. Don’t wait on Julian if it risks making you late.
3. **Give work a heads-up:** “My transportation fell through unexpectedly. I’m arranging a ride and will update you with my arrival time.”
4. **Make Maya’s stroller accessible before you leave.** Move it somewhere secure that her caregiver can reach, or give them access to the lock. You can protect your bike without blocking the stroller.

How long until you need to leave, and what ride options do you have?

Unlocked the garage. Maya can get the stroller. Julian texted back "it's just a bike." Not just a bike. It's my ride to work. I need help writing what I say to him tonight. Not some robot script. I won't call the landlord or the cops. And I won't hide behind Maya.

“It’s not ‘just a bike’ when it’s how I get to work. You took it without asking and left me stranded before my shift. Then when I told you the problem, you brushed it off. That pissed me off.

“I shouldn’t have to convince you that I need my own bike. You need to ask before taking it and wait for me to say yes. If I haven’t said yes, don’t take it. That’s what I need you to agree to tonight.”

If he keeps saying you’re making a big deal out of it:

“You don’t have to think it’s a big deal to respect that it’s mine. Are you going to ask first or not?”
That's not bad. But I'm not saying "that pissed me off" to him. He'll use that to call me emotional and change the subject. Give me something tighter. I need to own this, not defend it.

“You took my bike without asking and left me without a ride to work. Don’t take it again unless I’ve said yes. Calling it ‘just a bike’ doesn’t change that.”

If he changes the subject:

“I’m talking about my bike. You need my permission to use it.”
I'm not using "that pissed me off." He'll call me emotional and change the subject. Give me tighter. I need to own it, not defend it.

“My bike isn’t yours to take. Ask first, and wait for a yes.”

If he tries to sidetrack it:

“I’m not debating this. No yes, no bike.”
Bike isn't back. I'm taking an Uber to my shift. I'll confront him in person tonight at 8:30. Don't tell me to call the landlord or the cops. I'm doing this my way.

You’ve got your ride to work handled. For 8:30, keep it short:

“Bring my bike back tonight. You took my ride to work, so I had to pay for an Uber. I expect you to cover it. From now on, you ask and wait for a yes.”

If he deflects: “I’m not debating whether I need my bike. What time will it be back?”

You can be firm without staying in an argument. If he gets aggressive, step away—you don’t need to settle everything tonight.
